newsitem.title: USA: Fast U.S. planting pace may have banished $9 beans.
newsitem.headline: Fast U.S. planting pace may have banished $9 beans.

text.p: Rapid spring soybean planting and prospects for a record crop this fall lessened the chance that Chicago Board of Trade old-crop soybean futures would return to $9.00 per bushel, analysts said.
"We can't conjure up a new-crop supply problem. In fact getting it planted early many times gives way to better-than-trend yields," said Dale Gustafson, analyst with Smith Barney.
The U.S. Agriculture Department estimated farmers will harvest a record large 2.6 billion bushel crop this year.

In early trading Tuesday, CBOT soybeans for July delivery traded down 8-1/2 cents at $8.60 per bushel after dropping 20-1/2 cents Monday. Monday's slide was the sharpest one-day drop since April 11, and pushed values to the lowest close since April 30.
July soybeans peaked at $9.02 on May 7.

Gustafson does not rule out a return to $9.00 at the CBOT, but it would require problems with the U.S. crop or Brazil slashing exports or sharply raising soybean prices. Currently, Brazil soybeans are priced $22 per tonne less than U.S. beans, which should siphon export demand from the U.S., he said.
"I don't think we will see $9.00 again," said Dick Loewy, president of AgResource Co. "I think we will gradually trend lower."

Farmers still carrying memories of last year's rain-delayed plantings rushed planters through dry, albeit cold fields this spring. The USDA said as of Sunday, 20 percent of U.S. soybeans were planted, well ahead of eight percent a year ago and the 12 percent five-year average.
The cold soil may slow germination but at this point, farmers and grain analysts were optimistic for a healthy crop when warmer weather arrives.
Despite the bearishness of early plantings, Gustafson doubts soybean prices will move sharply lower until there is evidence exports and soybean processing have slowed.
"I think that's the thing that will keep us from getting too cheap," he said. "I suspect lower prices will find buyer interest."

If the current export and crush paces continue, it would suggest negative soybean supplies in USDA's supply and demand tables this summer, Gustafson said. But he believes old-crop exports will slow this summer as buyers either buy South American beans or wait for lower-priced new-crop U.S. soybeans.

USDA data showed the U.S. has shipped 85 percent of its expected 1996/97 soybean exports. Weekly exports for the next 15 weeks would have to average about 8.55 million bushels if exports are not to exceed USDA's 895-million-bushel export estimate.
From April 3 to May 8, soybean exports averaged 12.2 million bushels a week.
Mario Balletto, Merrill Lynch analyst, said USDA's crush estimate of 1.425 billion bushels suggests the crush will decrease.
"Their number indicates from here on out, the crush will go down two to three percent from a year ago," he said.

The U.S. Census Bureau data shows the crush from October to March averaged 10 percent more than a year ago. As of March, the total crush was more than half of USDA's total yearly crush with six months left in the crop year.
The Census Bureau's April data will be released May 22.
